extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters learning news/crime reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Examples and exemplar passages of police/crime news items illustrating how to report criminal incidents, arrests, burglaries, holds, and human-interest aftermaths for newspapers. Focuses on factual leads, sourcing, scene detail, quotations, and closure (arrests/charges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear factual lead (who/what/when/where/why)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the story with a concise lead that states the essential facts of the incident (what happened, where, and when) so readers immediately understand the news event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples open with lines like "Diamonds and other stones to the value of $3500 were stolen yesterday afternoon from the apartments of Mrs. Dennis M. Patrick" and "At 3:30 o'clock this afternoon the police were still investigating the lawyer." Use specific times/dates and the primary fact up front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include specific identifying details (names, ages, occupations, addresses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide names, ages, occupations, and often addresses for victims, suspects, and principal actors so the report is concrete and verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories routinely give details such as "Henry A. Black, 47, smart lawyer", "John E. Jones, jr., 21, a pallid bank bookkeeper", and addresses like "215 Wilson Place." These elements appear early and anchor the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute to authoritative sources (police, detectives, witnesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear where information comes from by attributing statements and facts to police, detectives, witnesses, or named officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases used include "the police said", "Detective M. T. Arey found", "the prosecutor said last night." Attribution signals reliability and permits reported claims to be checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations to convey voice and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate direct quotes from suspects, victims, police, family, or witnesses to reveal motive, emotion, or to provide firsthand perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations such as "I was the fool," "For God's sake get this money" and interview snippets from arrested men increase immediacy and show character. Use quotes for key reactions and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide scene and sensory detail to dramatize events
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the physical scene and sensory elements (smoke, fingerprints, a revolver, crowded train, hospital ward) to make the report vivid and readable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "a cigarette on the floor, a room full of smoke and an excellent set of finger prints on a hand mirror," or the hospital scene where "their year-old baby laughed and cooed." Use such details selectively to support the factual account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report chronological sequence and action (narrative flow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the events in clear sequence—how the crime unfolded, the pursuit/arrest, and immediate aftermath—so the reader can follow cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories recount step-by-step actions: how checks were passed leading to discovery; how robbers held up victims and were later arrested after running into a fence. Use time markers (e.g., "then," "after," times of day) to order events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give concrete numerical facts (amounts, counts, times)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include precise numbers where relevant—money stolen, number of items taken, times, ages, totals—to add factual weight and specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses specifics: "$9,800", "thirty-seven diamonds, eight emeralds and eight pearls", "$3,000", "12 holdups", and exact times like "2:30 o'clock." Avoid vague approximations when numbers are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note investigatory or procedural status (arrests, charges, custody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude or update items with the official procedural outcome: arrests made, charges to be filed, investigations continuing, hospital confinement, or pending arraignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples end with "were held in jail over night. Tomorrow both will be charged with a felony," "will be charged with highway robbery," and "Blair will be confined ... until he is physically able to be arraigned." This tells readers what comes next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background/context on individuals and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer concise background information (employment, family, prior troubles, financial strain) that helps explain motives or patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Black/Jones account gives business history and personal details to explain why deception occurred; the Blair piece narrates job loss, illness and poverty leading to crime. Use background that is relevant and verifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include physical evidence and investigative clues
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on tangible evidence or clues (fingerprints, cigarette, weapon, mask) found at the scene that support the account and the investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burglary story notes "an excellent set of finger prints on a hand mirror" and other items left behind; the holdup tale mentions a "black mask" found. Such details strengthen the factual basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance human-interest/emotional elements with factual reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanize the story with emotional scenes or quotations (weeping family, child's reaction) while keeping factual, sourced reporting as the backbone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes like "Black and Mrs. Black wept" or the hospital depiction of a baby on his father's pillow illustrate compassion and drama; include these elements to engage readers but avoid speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight community or official response and policy implications
rubrics_metrics.description: When relevant, record statements by officials or calls for action that place the incident in a wider civic or policy context (e.g., police deployment, public safety concerns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Little Italy piece quotes the chief of detectives saying "There should be at least four policemen in that district at night," linking crimes to policing levels. Use such commentary to inform on broader consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use episodic or feature-style structures for longer narrative pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: For longer or more literary crime pieces, organize the story into scenes or 'reels' to build tension and convey multiple perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One account is arranged in "REAL I, REAL II, REAL III," showing how episodic structure can dramatize a sequence of events. Employ scene labels and shifting viewpoints sparingly and when appropriate.
